name: Agent Blueprint

hlido_opinion.headline: A cleanly-designed CLI + MCP server that delivers implementation 'blueprints' to coding agents as Agent Skills directories — but the whole thing is gated behind a commercial engagement, so almost nothing about it is independently verifiable.
hlido_opinion.body: Agent Blueprint's developer surface does the agent-integration mechanics correctly. It ships an npm package ('npm install -g agentblueprint') that is both a CLI and a built-in MCP server, and it commits to the Agent Skills open standard — every blueprint exports as a SKILL.md-anchored directory that Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and other Agent-Skills-aware agents auto-discover. The MCP server exposes a sensible, well-named tool set (list_blueprints, get_blueprint, download_blueprint, get_use_case, get_business_case, get_implementation_plan, get_implementation_spec, get_business_profile) and the config snippet is a clean 'npx -y agentblueprint serve'. For an agent that needs structured implementation context for a platform build (the example given is ServiceNow), this is exactly the right shape of integration. The problem for an independent rating is that the product is not open: the page states plainly that 'API tokens are issued with an engagement; if your organization works with us, you're ready to go.' In other words, the npm package is a thin client for a consulting/platform engagement — without an engagement there is no token, no blueprints, and nothing to actually run. The captured surface is correspondingly sparse: no pricing, no self-serve access, no sample blueprint to inspect, no evidence of the blueprints' quality or coverage, and no track record visible. So while the plumbing looks professional and genuinely agent-native, Hlido can only vouch for the integration design, not for the value of what flows through it. This is a review of a gate, not of the product behind it.

tier_rationale: FADING (64) because the agent-integration design is genuinely good — a proper CLI + built-in MCP server, adherence to the Agent Skills open standard, and a clean, well-named tool surface — but the entire product is gated behind a commercial engagement (API tokens issued only 'with an engagement'), the public surface is thin, and there is no self-serve access, pricing, sample blueprint, or independent evidence of the blueprints' quality. Confidence is low: most of what would determine the product's actual worth sits behind the gate and cannot be verified from the surface. Not STEADY because so little is inspectable; not lower because what IS shown (the integration mechanics) is competent and honestly described.
what_it_does_well: Agent-native integration done right: an npm-installed CLI plus a built-in MCP server ('npx -y agentblueprint serve') for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and other MCP-compatible agents
Commits to the Agent Skills open standard — blueprints export as SKILL.md-anchored directories that Agent-Skills-aware coding agents auto-discover
Clean, sensibly-named MCP tool set (list/get/download blueprint, get use-case / business-case / implementation-plan / implementation-spec / business-profile)
Honest about the access model — it states up front that API tokens come with an engagement, rather than implying self-serve availability
what_it_fails_at: Gated behind a commercial engagement: API tokens are 'issued with an engagement', so without becoming a client there is no token, no blueprints and nothing to run
Thin public surface — no pricing, no self-serve signup, no sample blueprint to inspect, and no evidence of blueprint quality or coverage
Nothing about the actual deliverable (the implementation specs) is independently verifiable from the surface; Hlido can only assess the integration layer
No visible track record, customer evidence, or adoption signal on the captured page
best_for: Organizations already in (or entering) a delivery engagement with Agent Blueprint who want their coding agents to pull structured implementation specs in-editor
Teams standardizing on the Agent Skills format who value a first-class MCP + CLI path to structured platform-implementation context
Platform-implementation work (e.g. ServiceNow) where a vetted implementation spec delivered as an Agent Skills directory saves setup time
not_recommended_for: Anyone wanting a self-serve tool they can try today — access requires a commercial engagement and an issued API token
Buyers who need to inspect pricing, sample output, or independent quality evidence before committing
Individual developers or small teams without an engagement relationship — there is no free or open path to the blueprints
Use cases needing an open, inspectable knowledge base rather than a gated, engagement-bound one
red_flags: Core functionality is inaccessible without a commercial engagement (API tokens 'issued with an engagement'), and the public surface offers no pricing, sample, or self-serve path — so the product cannot be independently evaluated before purchase.

agent_relevance.agent_integration_path: A coding agent adds the MCP server via 'npx -y agentblueprint serve' (Claude Code / Cursor / Codex / MCP-compatible) and gains tools to list, fetch and download blueprints as Agent Skills directories; the CLI ('agentblueprint list' / 'download <id> --platform ...') does the same from the terminal. Both paths require an API token, which is issued only with a commercial engagement — so the integration is agent-native but not usable without becoming a client.

No pricing and no self-serve access — API tokens are 'issued with an engagement'
API-token auth on first CLI use; access bound to a commercial engagement
